docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Lövell is an application for Electronically-Assisted Visual Astronomy.

Lövell owes its existence to the amazing application Jocular, by @MartinCooke, and, to some extent, its successor, Canisp. The main display looks a bit like Canisp, the DSO and observations catalogues are lifted almost directly from Jocular (translated from Python to Lua.)

The novel thing about Lövell is that the image processing workflow is performed almost entirely within the GPU using code written in Open GL Shader Language. This makes it fast... most post-stack operations are performed within one video frame update (typically 1/60 second) so all interactive adjustments intensity / colour / filtering happen almost instantly.

Lövell does not control cameras, mounts, filter wheels, or similar equipment; plenty of other applications do this, such as APT, NINA, SharpCap, SG Pro, and ASI Studio. Instead, it watches a folder for one of these applications to drop raw FITS image files into, then processes them. The usual workflow is to store each new set of observation files in its own unique folder. Lövell maintains a database of previous observations so that they can be returned to and reprocessed with just the click of button.

The philosophy of Jocular — that just about everything aside from the exposure and framing of the individual incoming subs can be changed on the fly — remains central to the design:

  • preprocessing steps like hot pixel removal, applying calibration masters, and de-Bayering
  • stacking options of averaging or minimum variance
  • post-stack processing for luminance, chrominance, smoothing, and sharpening

...can all be changed or updated while new data continues to be acquired.

Note

Lövell is built on the LÖVE 2D platform, using Lua as a scripting language running under the LuaJit compiler. This explains the umlaut (ö) in the name, giving a nod to its software foundation, but also Sir Bernard Lovell, the creator and director of the Jodrell Bank radio telescope, which you can't deny is EAA on a grand scale, albeit with radio waves rather than visible ones. It also explains why the app's icon is a radio telescope, and not an optical one. There are also other famous Lovells, Jim, for example, of Apollo 8 and 13 fame. Using German pronunciation, Lövell sounds like the astronomer Percival Lowell, who founded the observatory in Flagstaff, AZ, and became infamous for sketching the Martian 'canals'.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Lövell maintains a number of databases to support its functionality:

  • DSOs
  • Observations
  • Calibration files
  • Telescopes
  • Cameras
  • FITS files headers

All databases are displayed in the form of spreadsheets, with column titles, column search filter boxes and, if required, a scrollbar. A 'Clear' button to the right hand side of these two header rows clears them to their reset values. A 'Close' button in the top left of the screen returns to the main display (also activated by typing the ESC key.) The button to the right of the 'Close' button, with the database name followed by an ellipsis (...) is a drop-down menu to access the other databases. Other controls may be scattered around the top and bottom margins to implement database-specific actions.

Clicking a column title button sorts the rows in a forward/reverse direction.

The search filters are of two main types: numeric and plain text, depending on the data shown in that column.

Text filters are case-insensitive and allow the '.' and '*' wildcard characters for a single character or any number of characters, respectively.

Numeric filters can be simply a number, in which case an exact match is required. Additionally, an inequality '<' or '>' may precede a numeric value to allow a search for values below or above a given threshold.

A right-click (or two-fingered click for touch input devices) clears the individual text box.

The usual line (de)selection methods are available by clicking on individual lines, shift-clicking to define a contiguous set of rows, or command-clicking to select discrete rows.

docs.title: DSOs
docs.text:
The DSO database provides a number of functionalities. At the basic level it contains some 40,000 objects of interest, with common identification features: name, object type, constellation, RA and DEC coordinates, magnitude and diameter. Additionally, some dynamic parameters are computed in real time: azimuth, altitude, maximum altitude, transit time, and location (which is a convenient octant-based indication of azimuth: N, NE, E, ...).

Selecting a single object and then the 'Set Current Object' button is one way to add the object details to the current observation.

A further feature is provision for observing watchlists. The number of recorded observations are displayed as well as the name of an observing list. To add an object, or multiple objects, select them in the usual spreadsheet way and then click 'Add to Watchlist'. Alternatively, remove them with the 'Remove from Watchlist' button. By default, following the Jocular modality, the watchlist is titled by today's date (eg. 25 Dec), but the text input box between the two watchlist buttons may be used to define any short list name. So it's possible to name any number of watchlists simultaneously, and you can move objects betwen lists by simply renaming them to the new list. An object can, of course, only be on one list at once. The search box for the 'List' column makes it especially easy to work through a list of targets.

The final function of this database is to provide an observation planner. The combination of watchlists, dynamic parameters of azimuth and elevation (and octant) and column filters, allow you to plan and organise a viewing session. For example, you could select the objects on a particular watchlist which are above 45 degrees elevation, in an easterly direction, and ordered in transit time, making it very easy to pick them off one by one with a minimum of mount movement. One powerful extra tool here is the horizontal slider which allows up to 24 hours to be added to the current time, so that you can plan in advance of an evening's session where the targets will be at the time you plan to observe. The dynamic parameters are instantly recomputed for the set time, and also the elevation of the sun. A right-click on this slider resets its value to zero, hence back the current time.

Tip

As a bonus 'Easter Egg', double-clicking on an object which has at least one recorded observation will take you to the Observations database showing just those observations...

Note

If you've used Jocular, then this should seem very familiar, because 95% of the implementation code has been ported directly from there, with just a few tiny additional enhancements.

docs.title: Observations
docs.text:
A list of previous observations. It includes the session number (date in YYYYMMDD format) and local time, number of exposures and average exposure, Bayer pattern (if an OSC camera with a CFA) and image size, name of the telescope, if known, and any observation notes you may have added.

Filtering and sorting of columns works as standard (ie. as for the DSOs). Selecting an observation row allows you to load that data using the 'Load Observation' button, or visit its folder of raw subs on disk with the 'Go To Folder' button.

Tip

Double clicking on a row instantly starts loading that observation in the same way as the 'Load Observation' button.

docs.title: Calibration files
docs.text:
Bias, Darks, and Flats to be applied in the calibration of incoming images.

Warning

The handling of calibration master files is under review/development. The screen may not look exactly like this.

docs.title: FITS file headers
docs.text:
Unlike the other databases, this is not persistent between sessions, but is build dynamically from the file headers of incoming images for the current observation. Depending on the acquisition software being used, this may have details of the image format, filters, cameras, mount positioning, temperature, and other parameters. If present, some of the key values are extracted and stored in the observations database.

Tip

This example has been sorted by the 'Name' field, which makes it much easier to find a given parameter.

The header data from every sub in the observation is available to view here, you can just scroll through the frames with the horizontal slider.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
This really is very easy . The Lövell install consists of two parts:

  • LÖVE – a framework for making 2D games. It's free, open-source, and works on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS.

  • Lövell app – written in the Lua language.

Note

The LÖVE runtime image is tiny by modern standards – around 25 Mbytes – and the Lövell package itself is, remarkably, only about 1 Mbyte. Of course, when running, considerable CPU/GPU memory may be used to store images.

docs.title: Download LÖVE application
docs.text: You can find the appropriate (Mac, Linux, or PC) image here https://love2d.org/#download and it downloads in just one click.

docs.title: Install LÖVE
docs.text: Install it, per the relevant instructions, which places it in your Applications folder or similarly appropriate place for your system.

docs.title: Download Lövell
docs.text:
Download the Lövell.love file from this repository, and put it in a suitable place. You may need to click on it or drop a folder onto it to start the application.

Note

LÖVE 2D packages the LuaJit interpreter/compiler and a compiler for OpenGL Shader Language (GLSL) which gives access to the GPU for image processing operations.

Lua is a powerful, efficient, lightweight, embeddable scripting language. Several benchmarks show Lua to be the fastest among interpreted scripting languages.

LuaJit is a Just-In-Time Compiler (JIT) for the Lua programming language (makling it even faster!)

docs.title: The LÖVE environment
docs.text:
LÖVE is, by design, a framework for running interactive 2D games which must, inherently, handle fast graphics and a very flexible user interface. The design choice to use it for Lövell arises from its support of both the Lua language, and the OpenGL Shader Language (GLSL), giving integrated access to the platform's Graphic Processing Unit (GPU).

The LÖVE environment generally discourages reading or writing arbitrary parts of the user's file system, reserving a very specific set of locations for these actions. Using the LÖVE filesystem, the only external files or folders that may be read are those which have been actively dropped onto the running application, and the only folder which may be written is system specific:

System The SAVE directory Windows C:\Users\user\AppData\Roaming\LOVE Mac OS /Users/user/Library/Application Support/LOVE/ Linux $XDG_DATA_HOME/love/ Android /data/data/org.love2d.android/files/save/

docs.title: Lövell's use of disk storage
docs.text:
The contraints that LÖVE brings with it have guided Lövell's design choices:

  • no files are ever written to the folders where the acquired FITS files reside
  • calbration master files are copied into a Master folder in the SAVE directory area (why? ...so they are available to apply to future dropped folders of lights)

Lövell creates a set of files and folders in the SAVE Directory to hold its metadata:

file/folder function masters/ calibration files: bias / dark / flat snapshots/ saved PNG screenshots sessions/ one JSON file per session (day) with observation metadata platesolve/ working files for the ASTAP platesolver settings/ reserved for future use settings.json current Lövell application defaults Lövell.log logfile for the current (or previous) session

Tip

The Settings page in Lövell gives easy shortcuts to some of these folders which can be browsed by the usual utilities (Preview, Finder, ...)

docs.title: Reporting issues
docs.text:
The best way to report a genuine issue with Lövell is to open an issue on GitHub at https://github.com/akbooer/Lovell/issues.

For things more in the way of comments or seeking advice, both Stargazer's Lounge and Cloudy Nights are an option.

docs.title: The Main Display
docs.text: The main display shows a stacked image with controls for adjustments and an information panel.

docs.title: Image area
docs.text:
The central image area has two formats. By default an eyepiece view is shown, a circular window onto generally the central portion of the image. Alternatively, a rectangular (landscape) view of the image can be chosen. The eyepiece view ('ocular') is stolen from Jocular for good reasons: it serves to focus the attention on the object of interest; it hides the corners of the image where optical abberations such as vignetting and coma are prevalent; it allows manual rotation of the image by clicking and dragging the border which is highlighted when hovered; and it evokes a 'through the telescope' or possibly 'spaceship porthole' aesthetic.

The control panel button in the lower left shows the current mode 'Eyepiece...' or 'Landscape...' and may be toggled by clicking on it. Either view may be moved by clicking and dragging on the central part of the image. The zoom level may be changed with a scroll gesture (mouse wheel / two-fingered drag on a touch pad).

The checkboxes in the same left-hand corner may be used to flip the image vertically or horizontally to get a preferred view.

Tip

There are also keyboard shortcuts to change the view:

Command-E is Eyepiece, Command-L Landscape, and Command-T toggles between them.

Command-'-' and Command-'+' zoom out and in.

Command-'/' and Command-'\' rotate clockwise and anti-clockwise.

For a full list of keyboard shortcuts see that section in the documentation.

docs.title: Control Panel
docs.text:
The control panel on the left hand side is mostly populated by buttons which display menus when clicked or hovered. Many of these controls are plugins, which provide parameter adjustments for various different processing steps. Some of them are permanently in place (static), others (dynamic) may be configured, moved around, or removed completely and replaced by others, through a separate Plugin Workflow editor page.

Additionally, many of the plugin menus have a checkbox which splits the controls between those which are retained in the drop-down and others which are moved to appead below the button and are visible and accessible all the time. This flexibility means that the order of the menu buttons, and the screen appearance, may vary depending on their configuration. However, there are four main functional areas:

static

docs.title: 1. Channel, Luminance/Midtone, Chroma/RGB
docs.text:
This group largely controls how the final stacked and processed image is rendered. The Channel menu with LRGB as a default shows a full colour image (if any). Other options show just the luminance or individual Red / Green / Blue channels, and also a photographic 'negative' view of the luminance – sometimes helpful in detecting low contrast features in some targets.

Midtone is one of several stretch functions MidTone / Asinh / Hyper / Linear / Log / Gamma / ... which may be selected from that menu. RGB is one of several chroma processing modes.

The Luminance menu drops down to show gradient / vignette / white point sliders plus the main controls of background level and stretch amount.

The Chroma show controls for tint / SCNR (green) and the main controls of colour saturation and temperature for the RGB option. Other chroma modes (HSO) have their own different controls.

Tip

The Luminance and Chroma menus may be 'split' using the checkboxes halfway down each menu. This keeps the major controls showing in the panel beneath their respective buttons, even if their menus are not hovered.

Tip

Double-clicking on the image itself also toggles the normal/inverted mode.

docs.title: 2. Post-stack processing
docs.text:
The next group shows a series of post-processing options, implemented by dynamic plugins. These are selected with the Plugin workflow editor page, where the sequence and type of post-stack processing can be configured. This section, then, may have a difference appearance from that imaged.

This group begins with the SynthL plugin which is the first step in the post-stack workflow, constructing a synthetic luminance from separate RGB (and/or HSO) and L stacks, which may then be applied to whatever chroma processing has been selected. In general, however, the following plugins include steps to smooth, sharpen, and refine the image. Such options as Bilateral filtering, sharpening, contrast enhancement may be configured. Other plugins include additional colour saturation processing and statistical parameters from the stack.

docs.title: 3. Pre-stack and stacking
docs.text:
Prestack / Stack menus give options for those stages of processing.

Databases gives access to various catalogs, etc.

docs.title: 4. Display format
docs.text:
Button to toggle between Eyepiece and Landscape layouts.

Checkboxes to flip image in either axis.

Snapshot button, see Snapshots.

Note

The flip checkbox settings are over-ridden by the Platesolve plugin, along with the image rotation, in order to correctly orient the image as North-up / East-left.

docs.title: Information Panel
docs.text:
Input field to name the object.

Other useful info

docs.title: Panel Controls
docs.text:
A small cluster of controls at the lower right-hand corner of the screen provides a button to switch to the Settings page, a button to Exit the application, and a label showing the current day and local time (so you don't stay up too late observing).

Tip

Command-Q will also close Lövell, and on Mac OS command-W (close window) too.

Command-M, on a Mac, will minimise the window to the dock.

docs.title: Plate Solving
docs.text:
Plate solving is the action of locating the exact coordinates (such as right ascension and declination) of an astronomical image, by matching it to known star locations. Additionaly, the image scale, and camera orientation may be solved. Given a camera with known pixel size, the exact focal length of the optical system may be determined. This is often done as a prelude to annotating the image with known deep space object identifiers.

In Lövell, plate solving is achieved through an external program called ASTAP, which has to be installed separately.

docs.title: ASTAP Installation
docs.text:
Installers for all the major operating systems and machine architectures are available here https://www.hnsky.org/astap.htm. Select the appropriate one for your system.

Additionally it requires a star database to be downloaded, also available at that site. There's several to choose from depending on your equipment and needs. I used the D20 one.

docs.title: Platesolve plugin
docs.text: The platesolve plugin is static (permanently installed).

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text: Much of Lövell's functionality is implemented as separate processing modules called plugins. There are of two types: Static or Dynamic. There is a separate Plugin workflow editor page, which allows dynamic plugins to be (de)selected and placed in order into the post-stack workflow, appearing as dropdown menus on the main display page.

docs.title: Static Plugins
docs.text: Static plugins are part of the system workflow and, as such, are permanently installed

docs.title: Hubble
docs.text:
HUBBLE (pseudo-SHO) based on Bill Blanshan's "Narrowband Normalization" PixInsight code.

This treats RGB channels as HSO and swizzles them to be SHO ordered.

The controls are specfic to his process and more details can be found online, but feel free to experiment, the names are fairly self-explanatory.

docs.title: Dynamic Plugins
docs.text: Dynamic plugins may be picked to appear in the post-stack workflow processing chain. Simply drag and drop into a blank location in the post-processing chain column. Valid locations are highlighted as you drag. To remove a plugin from the processing workflow, simply drag and drop it away from the workflow column and it will snap back to its reserved location in the plugin list.

docs.title: Generalised Hyperbolic Stretch (GHS)
docs.text:
An altogether better way of stretching images.

This stretch is applied after any of the built-in stretches.

docs.title: Contrast Limited Adaptive Histogram Enhancement (CLAHE)
docs.text: Another way to effectively sharpen an image by increasing its contrast in different areas,

docs.title: Sharpen
docs.text: Sharpening method based on the ideas of APF-R

docs.title: Quick Tour
docs.text:
• click on the Lövell.love file (or drop onto the LÖVE app) to run it
  • drop a folder containing raw 16-bit FITS files onto the app window...
  • ...the folder is continuously watched for new FITS files appearing.

docs.title: Main display
docs.text:
The main display shows a stacked image with controls for adjustments and an information panel. Most buttons are drop-down menus (which remain pinned if clicked rather than hovered.)

  • Channel: LRGB menu views LRGB / Mono / Inverted / Red / Green / Blue channels individually
  • Hyper is one of several stretch functions MidTone / Asinh / Hyper / Linear / Log / Gamma / ...
  • Luminance menu drops down to show additional gradient / vignette / white point sliders
  • background / stretch are the main luminance controls (right- or shift- click set to default)
  • RGB* menu also includes Hubble (SHO) and possibly other colour processing options
  • Chroma menu drops down to show additional tint / SCNR (green) sliders
  • saturation / temperature are the main chrominance controls for the RGB option
  • SynthL / Balance / Bilateral / Sharpen / CLAHE / etc. are controls for optional processing plugins
  • Prestack / Stack menus give options for those stages of processing
  • Databases (shown dropped down) gives access to various catalogs, etc.
  • mouse wheel / trackpad scroll zooms the display
  • click and drag moves the display
  • click on Eyepiece.. to switch to Landscape.. display, and vice versa
  • hover over eyepiece ring to activate image rotation, click and drag to change
  • enter object name in field on top right to search DSO catalogue

docs.title: DSO / Observation list
docs.text:
Some 40,000 objects of interest. Close button returns to main display.

  • click on column names to sort
  • text or numeric expressions in filter boxes to select subsets
  • click, shift-click, option/control-click to (de)select multiple items
  • hover over menu button 'DB: ...' to show menu of other dabases: DSO / Observations / Watch list / ...
  • scroll control to forward time by up to 24 hours, updating object positions in Az, Alt, etc...

docs.title: View stack/subs
docs.text:
View all the subs in sequence, show detected and matched stars. Close button returns to main display.

  • mouse wheel / trackpad to scroll through subs
  • Stretch applies a variable screen stretch to the display
  • Play button animates sequence of subs
  • rate control changes speed
  • Blink toggles between adjacent subs
  • Show stars indicates detected stars (in blue) and those matched for alignment (orange)

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: The Settings page provides a useful home for a number of less-used input fields and buttons.

docs.title: Defaults
docs.text: The first button row provides a way to define your preference for the startup values of the Stack and Stretch menus, and also a checkbox which retains all plugin control settings between different observations (but not between separate sessions). Otherwise they are reset to their default initial values for each observation.

docs.title: Optical system
docs.text:
Some details of the optical system are settable here. Most decent acquisition software will define the camera pixel size in the FITS headers, but may not include the focal length which is a key parameter in plate solving.

Note

If the pixel size is not defined, plate solving will not be able to determine the correct image scale. If focal length is missing, or wrong, plate solving (ASTAP) may attempt a number of different scales and can still correctly solve the image. For all successful solves, the focal length is changed to the solved value and stored in the observation metadata so that it is correct when next loaded.

docs.title: Observation and Session notes
docs.text:
Short observations notes are shown on the information panel on the main display, and cleared between observations. The may also be shown in some snapshot format.

Short sessions notes are retained for the whole session over multiple observations and, again, shown on the main display page.

Tip

Each of the above items has a Clear button to delete all the input, but this may also be achieved by right-clicking the input box (two-fingered click for touch input devices).

docs.title: Navigation buttons
docs.text:
The open log file button uses the system's document browser to access the current session log file which is opened in a separate window. The file is located in the Lövell's SAVE directory (see Installation)

The open snapshot folder button provides a fast way to access previous screen snapshots stored in Lövell's SAVE directory in the snapshots folder. It opens with the system file browser in a separate window.

The open masters folder similarly opens the calibration master files folder in the SAVE directory.

The configure plugins button is an internal link to the Plugin Workflow Editor page.

Tip

The workflow editor may also be accessed with the keyboard shortcut command-P.

docs.title: Location coordinates
docs.text:
Latitude and longitude (negative for west of the meridian) may be entered here. It's essential to do this for the DSO database to show the correct RA and DEC coordinates.

Note

Currnet local time is taken from your system's settings.

docs.title: Signature for Snapshots
docs.text:
Annotated snapshots include a line for a 'signature'. The text is adjustable here and saved between sessions.

Note

The application version is also shown on this page. Maybe useful if you need to report an issue.

docs.title: Keyboard Shortcuts
docs.text: There are keyboard shortcuts for a number of different actions. Some of them work from any page, others are specific to a particular one.

docs.title: Global Shortcuts
docs.text:
The user interface components are somewhat different from the standard ones used, so to augment their functionality there are some mouse/key based shortcuts:

  • right-click on any text input field clears any current text
  • right-click (or shift-click) resets slider or menu controls to their default

For spreadsheet tables:

  • left-click selects an item
  • shift click selects a contiguous set of items between cursor and previous selection
  • command-click adds or removes single selecterd item from the current selection
  • double-click generally performs some table-specific action

Tip

ESC key returns to the main display from any page

Command- or Ctrl- depending on operating system:

⌘-Key Action C Calibration masters database D DSO database E Eyepiece mode F FITS headers L Landscape mode O Observations database P Plugin workflow editor S Settings page V View stack of subs

docs.title: Page-dependent Shortcuts
docs.text: ⌘-Key Action T Toggle between Eyepiece and Landscape mode 7 Scale to fill screen, possibly cropping one axis 8 Scale to fill screen, possibly leaving a margin 9 Fit to margins between control and information panels 0 Full size - one image pixel is one screen pixel + Zoom in – Zoom out . Rotate_to_zero / Rotate_clockwise, +90º \ Rotate_anticlockwise, -90º

docs.title: Snapshots
docs.text:
The Snapshot button on the lower left of the main display screen captures a PNG image of the current object and saves it in the snapshots folder in Lövell's SAVE directory (easily accessed through the Settings page).

Three different styles of capture are available:

  1. Eyepiece, with annotation
  2. Landscape, with annotation
  3. Full Resolution, unannotated

The style used for 1 & 2 matches the current viewing mode. To get option 3, hold the Option key down before pressing Snapshot in either display mode. The button annotation will change to Large PNG whilst the option button remains pressed.

The Eyepiece snapshot mirrors the look on the display, retaining its translation, flip, zoom, and rotation settings. The Landscape mode always shows the full extent of the stacked image (including any ragged margins which may arise from target tracking between frames) without rotation or zoom (but the vertical and horizontal flips are applied), as does the full-resolution capture.

Tip

These captures are all PNG files, since that is the only common format which LÖVE currently supports. The full resolution can be quite large (~50 Mbyte), but it's easy to reformat them with the usual system utilities. (I could generate a JPG by spawning an external process, but that's system-dependent and I haven't seen the need, yet.)

docs.title: Full Resolution
docs.text:
Note

Just for fun (another 'Easter Egg') the snapshot action has a shutter sound effect.

docs.title: Stack Viewer
docs.text:
View all the subs in sequence, show detected and matched stars.

Close button returns to main display.

This is a thumbnail view of all the images in this observation so far. OSC frames are de-Bayered, but all others (filtered or otherwise) are shown in mono. A vertical scroll bar on the right of the images may be used to traverse the stack, and up and down keyboard arrows also move through the subs.

The Stretch slider applies a variable screen stretch to the display, allowing fainter details to be shown, or supressing them to make the identified stars more visible against the background.

The Play button animates sequence of subs, moving forwards and backwards through the stack sequentially. The rate control changes the speed.

Blink stops any play in progress and toggles between adjacent subs, allowing a visual inspection of the differences.

Stop halts either Play or Toggle modes.

The Show stars buttons indicates detected stars (in blue) and those matched for alignment (orange).

Whilst viewing a particular sub, it may be removed from (or added back to) the stack by the omit from stack checkbox. Any changes made will cause a restack upon returning to the main display screen.

The aligment details show the translation (x, y) and image rotation 0.00º of the current sub, relative to the image centre of the first sub in the stack.

docs.title: Process Workflow Editor
docs.text:
The Plugin workflow editor page (command-P) allows dynamic plugins to be (de)selected and placed in order into the post-stack workflow, appearing as dropdown menus on the main display page.

Note

The modular plugin architecture allows for (relatively) easy processing extensions to be added to Lövell. Each plugin is a classic MVC (model-view-control) structure containing its own controls, GUI, processing (probably implemented as a GLSL shader plus Lua code), and brief documentation.

This page is divided into four column areas:

  • Static plugins
  • Dynamic plugins
  • Processing workflow
  • Information area

docs.title: Static Plugins
docs.text:
Static plugins are permanently installed parts of the processing chain and provide the basic elements of prestack and stacking workflow.

Hovering over a plugin will show its menu layout and some textual help in the information area.

docs.title: Dynamic Plugins
docs.text: Dynamic plugins are all configurable steps in the post-stack workflow. The may be drag and dropped onto empty positions in the workflow chain. As soon as you start dragging a plugin, all possible (empty) destinations in the chain are highlighted. Dropping the plugin on one of these locations enables its processing at that point in the workflow. Dropping elsewhere allows the plugin to snap back into its home position, removing it from the chain.

docs.title: Processing Workflow
docs.text:
This chain of plugin processes defines the post-stack workflow. It is performed in order, top to bottom, with empty steps being ignored. The order is also used in the main display to arrange the menu button in two columns of the control panel.

Below the main chain, the Clear All button will remove all configured plugins from the processing chain so that you can start afresh. The Factory Reset button returned to the initial default configuration.

The workflow is retained between separate Lövell runs.

docs.title: Information Area
docs.text:
This shows the menu layout of the selected plugin, and also its display name and filename. The static and dynamic columns are sorted by filename, which is unique between plugins, whereas the plugin display name (ID) is not unique. This is because plugins can provide alternative implementations of the same post-stack processing step. CHROMA is one such class of plugins, with RGB and HSO (and possibly others) being options.

Some help text for the controls is shown to the right of the menu layout. All plugin menus may be pinned with a checkbox in the top right-hand corner of the menu, so that they remain displayed even when not hovered. Some menus have an additional checkbox between two groups of controls. Checking this splits out from the menu the items below it, to appear permanently in the main display control panel beneath the plugin button. This is to allow the major (frequently used) controls to remain visible at all times, for easy access.

Note

Due to the configurability of the workflow, the main display will, inevitably, change appearance, so some screen shots in this documentation may not exactly match what you see.
